title: (Scenario) Partition leaders are moving frequently (due to rebalances, broker instability, or maintenance) — what is the impact: increased produce/consume latency (clients must refresh metadata and retry on NOT_LEADER_FOR_PARTITION), more errors and retries, consumer lag increases during leader transitions, higher broker load from coordination (metadata updates, ISR changes), and risk to durability if replicas fall out of ISR leaving fewer in-sync copies — and how do you stabilize it (fix the root cause of instability, avoid unnecessary preferred-leader elections, monitor leader count per broker)?
shortTitle: (Scenario) Partition leaders are moving frequently — what is the impact, and how do you stabilize it?

s1_definition.profdef: Every Kafka partition has one leader replica that serves all reads and writes, and followers replicate from it. When leaders move frequently, due to broker instability, rebalances, or maintenance, clients repeatedly hit NOT_LEADER_FOR_PARTITION errors, must refresh metadata and retry, which raises produce and consume latency and error rates, increases consumer lag during each transition, loads the brokers with coordination work from metadata updates and in-sync replica changes, and risks durability if replicas drop out of the in-sync set and leave fewer in-sync copies. You stabilize it by fixing the underlying instability, avoiding unnecessary preferred-leader elections, and monitoring the leader count per broker.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine each type of account at National Bank of India has one designated master branch that handles all its transactions, with backup branches keeping copies. If the master branch for an account keeps changing from one branch to another every few minutes, chaos follows. Customers who walk into the old master branch are told "this account is now handled elsewhere," so they waste time finding the new branch and retrying, which makes every transaction slower and more error-prone. The backlog of unprocessed transactions grows during each handover. Head office is constantly rewriting the master directory, which is extra work for everyone. And if a backup branch falls behind on its copies during all the churn, the account now has fewer safe copies, risking data loss. The cure is to find out why the master keeps changing, stop triggering unnecessary reassignments, and keep an eye on how many accounts each branch is master for.
s1_definition.oneliner: Frequent leader movement means repeated NOT_LEADER_FOR_PARTITION errors, metadata refreshes, retries, lag bumps, coordination load, and shrinking in-sync replicas — stabilize by fixing the root cause, avoiding needless preferred-leader elections, and monitoring leader count per broker.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Every Kafka partition has one leader replica that serves all reads and writes, and followers replicate from it. When leaders move frequently, due to broker instability, rebalances, or maintenance, clients repeatedly hit NOT_LEADER_FOR_PARTITION errors, must refresh metadata and retry, which raises produce and consume latency and error rates, increases consumer lag during each transition, loads the brokers with coordination work from metadata updates and in-sync replica changes, and risks durability if replicas drop out of the in-sync set and leave fewer in-sync copies. You stabilize it by fixing the underlying instability, avoiding unnecessary preferred-leader elections, and monitoring the leader count per broker.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine each type of account at National Bank of India has one designated master branch that handles all its transactions, with backup branches keeping copies. If the master branch for an account keeps changing from one branch to another every few minutes, chaos follows. Customers who walk into the old master branch are told "this account is now handled elsewhere," so they waste time finding the new branch and retrying, which makes every transaction slower and more error-prone. The backlog of unprocessed transactions grows during each handover. Head office is constantly rewriting the master directory, which is extra work for everyone. And if a backup branch falls behind on its copies during all the churn, the account now has fewer safe copies, risking data loss. The cure is to find out why the master keeps changing, stop triggering unnecessary reassignments, and keep an eye on how many accounts each branch is master for.

**One line to remember:** Frequent leader movement means repeated NOT_LEADER_FOR_PARTITION errors, metadata refreshes, retries, lag bumps, coordination load, and shrinking in-sync replicas — stabilize by fixing the root cause, avoiding needless preferred-leader elections, and monitoring leader count per broker.

sections.s2_technical:
First, understand the leader's central role. For each partition, exactly one replica is the leader, and all produce and consume requests go to the leader; followers only replicate. Clients cache cluster metadata that maps each partition to its current leader broker. When a leader moves, that cached mapping is stale, so the first impact is that a client sending to the old leader gets a NOT_LEADER_FOR_PARTITION error, must fetch fresh metadata to learn the new leader, and then retry the request against it. Each such cycle adds latency and shows up as a transient error, and when leaders move constantly, clients spend a meaningful fraction of their time refreshing metadata and retrying instead of doing useful work.

Second, consumer lag increases during transitions. While a leader is moving, the affected partition is briefly unavailable for consumption, and consumers must reconnect to the new leader. During that window, no progress is made on that partition, so lag ticks up each time, and if leaders move frequently, these repeated small stalls accumulate into noticeable lag and latency. Producers similarly buffer and retry during the gap, which can cause bursts once the new leader is available.

Third, broker coordination load rises. Leadership is tracked by the controller, and every leader change triggers metadata updates that must propagate to all brokers and clients, plus any in-sync replica set changes that accompany the move. This bookkeeping is normally cheap but becomes significant when it happens repeatedly across many partitions, stealing broker capacity from serving traffic and sometimes feeding a vicious cycle where the load from churn causes more instability.

Fourth, and most seriously, durability risk. When leadership churns, especially if it is driven by brokers flapping in and out of the cluster, follower replicas can fall out of the in-sync replica set because they cannot keep up during the disruption. A partition that normally has three in-sync replicas can temporarily drop to two or one. If it drops to one and your durability relies on at least two in-sync replicas, writes are either rejected or, if misconfigured, acknowledged on a single copy, which is the durability hole covered by the acks and min-in-sync-replicas contract. So frequent leader movement is not just a latency problem; it can quietly erode your replication safety.

The stabilization steps follow the root causes. The first and most important is to fix the underlying instability rather than treating symptoms. Common root causes include brokers under memory pressure doing long garbage-collection pauses that make them miss heartbeats and get kicked out, undersized or saturated disks and network causing replication to fall behind, flaky hardware or network links, and misconfigured timeouts such as too-short ZooKeeper or controller session timeouts that evict healthy-but-slow brokers. You diagnose with broker logs, garbage-collection logs, and metrics for under-replicated partitions, in-sync replica shrink and expand rates, and leader election rate, then address the specific cause, for example by tuning the JVM heap and garbage collector, adding capacity, replacing bad hardware, or correcting timeouts.

The second stabilization step is to avoid unnecessary preferred-leader elections. Kafka has a notion of a preferred leader, the first replica in a partition's assignment, and it periodically rebalances leadership back to the preferred leader to keep load even. If auto leader rebalancing is too aggressive, or if you trigger manual preferred-leader elections carelessly, you cause avoidable leader movement. You can disable or tune the automatic rebalance and only run preferred-leader elections deliberately during calm windows, so leadership moves when you intend it to, not constantly. The relevant broker setting is auto leader rebalance enable and its imbalance threshold and check interval.

The third stabilization step is monitoring the leader count per broker. A healthy cluster has leadership spread fairly evenly across brokers. If you watch the leader count per broker over time, you can see churn as the counts bouncing around, spot a broker that keeps losing and regaining leadership (a sign it is flapping), and detect imbalance where one broker carries too many leaders and becomes a hotspot. This metric, together with the leader election rate and under-replicated partition count, tells you both that churn is happening and often which broker is at fault. Here are the commands:

```bash
# See leader distribution and which partitions are under-replicated
kafka-topics.sh --describe --under-replicated-partitions --bootstrap-server kafka-1:9092

# Trigger a preferred-leader election DELIBERATELY, only when the cluster is calm
kafka-leader-election.sh --bootstrap-server kafka-1:9092 --election-type preferred --all-topic-partitions
```

Senior-level nuances: set generous but correct session and heartbeat timeouts so a briefly slow broker is not evicted, which prevents a flap-and-recover loop; keep brokers' garbage collection pauses short because long pauses are a leading cause of spurious evictions; stagger maintenance so you never take down enough brokers to force mass leadership movement; and treat a rising leader election rate as a first-class alert, because it is the earliest signal that something is making leadership unstable before it turns into latency and durability problems.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India's cluster began showing frequent leader movement after a memory-pressure issue made one broker pause for long garbage collections, repeatedly missing heartbeats and getting evicted and re-added. Settlement producers and consumers suffered. Rajesh and Priya transfers flow through the affected partitions.

Problem 1 — every time the flapping broker lost and regained leadership, producers and consumers got NOT_LEADER_FOR_PARTITION, refreshed metadata, retried, and lag bumped, so latency and error rates rose and settlement throughput dropped. This is the client-facing impact.

Problem 2 — during the churn, follower replicas fell out of the in-sync set, dropping some partitions to a single in-sync copy, which threatened durability. This is the durability-risk impact, and it forced us to prioritize stabilizing rather than just retrying harder.

Our runnable demo models a `Broker` that can flap, a `PartitionLeadership` tracker, and a `ClientImpact` model that counts NOT_LEADER errors, metadata refreshes, retries, lag, and in-sync replica shrink as leaders move, then shows the improvement after we stop the flapping and disable aggressive auto-rebalance. The classes are `LeaderChurnDemo`, `Broker`, `PartitionLeadership`, and `ClientImpact`.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a cluster where broker-2 is the leader for several settlement partitions and keeps flapping due to long garbage-collection pauses.

Step 1: Broker-2 pauses for a long garbage collection, misses its heartbeats, and the controller declares it dead and moves leadership of its partitions to other brokers. Moments later broker-2 recovers and rejoins, and because it is the preferred leader, leadership often moves back. This bounce repeats.

Step 2: Each time leadership moves, settlement producers and consumers that were talking to the old leader get NOT_LEADER_FOR_PARTITION, refresh cluster metadata, discover the new leader, and retry. This adds latency, raises the error rate, and wastes client time on metadata work.

Step 3: During each transition the affected partitions are briefly unavailable, so consumers make no progress and lag bumps up each cycle. Producers buffer and retry, then burst once the new leader is available, adding jitter to end-to-end timing.

Step 4: The controller does repeated metadata and in-sync replica bookkeeping for every move, loading the brokers, and during the churn some follower replicas fall out of the in-sync set, dropping partitions toward a single in-sync copy and threatening durability.

Step 5: After we fix the root cause by tuning the heap and garbage collector so broker-2 no longer pauses, and after disabling the overly aggressive automatic leader rebalancing, leadership stops moving. NOT_LEADER errors, refreshes, retries, lag bumps, and coordination operations all fall to near zero, and the in-sync replica set stays full, restoring both performance and durability.

Final output:

```
[2026-10-25 02:00:44] [INFO] === Unstable: broker-2 flapping (long GC pauses) ===
[2026-10-25 02:00:44] [SEVERE] UNSTABLE: NOT_LEADER=500 refreshes=500 retries=500 lagBump=20000 coordOps=100 ISR_SHRINK=10 (DURABILITY AT RISK)
[2026-10-25 02:00:44] [INFO] === Stabilized: fixed GC, disabled aggressive auto-rebalance ===
[2026-10-25 02:00:44] [INFO] STABILIZED: NOT_LEADER=0 refreshes=0 retries=0 lagBump=0 coordOps=0 ISR_SHRINK=0 (stable)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Every Kafka partition has exactly one leader replica that serves all reads and writes, and clients cache a map of which broker leads each partition. When leaders move frequently, that cache is constantly stale, and the impacts cascade. First, clients sending to the old leader get NOT_LEADER_FOR_PARTITION errors, must refresh metadata to find the new leader, and retry, which raises produce and consume latency and error rates and wastes client time. Second, each transition briefly makes the partition unavailable, so consumers stall and lag bumps up every cycle, and producers buffer and burst. Third, the controller does repeated metadata and in-sync replica bookkeeping for every move, which loads the brokers and can feed a vicious cycle. Fourth and most seriously, during the churn follower replicas can fall out of the in-sync set, dropping a partition toward a single in-sync copy, which erodes durability, so frequent leader movement is not just a latency problem but a safety problem.

On the National Bank of India cluster this happened when one broker was under memory pressure and kept pausing for long garbage collections, missing heartbeats, getting evicted, and rejoining, so leadership bounced every few minutes. Settlement producers and consumers suffered the NOT_LEADER errors, retries, and lag bumps, and some partitions dropped to a single in-sync replica, which is what forced us to prioritize stabilizing rather than just configuring more retries.

Stabilizing has three parts. The most important is fixing the underlying instability rather than its symptoms, which means diagnosing the real cause, often long garbage-collection pauses, saturated disk or network, flaky hardware, or timeouts set too short that evict healthy-but-slow brokers, and then addressing it specifically, such as tuning the heap and garbage collector, adding capacity, or correcting timeouts. The second is avoiding unnecessary preferred-leader elections, because Kafka periodically rebalances leadership back to the preferred leader, and if that automatic rebalancing is too aggressive or you trigger manual elections carelessly, you cause avoidable movement, so I disable or tune the automatic rebalance and only run preferred-leader elections deliberately during calm windows. The third is monitoring the leader count per broker along with the leader election rate and under-replicated partition count, because an even leader distribution is healthy, bouncing counts reveal churn, and a broker that keeps losing and regaining leadership is clearly flapping.

The nuances I always add are to set generous but correct session and heartbeat timeouts so a briefly slow broker is not evicted and thrown into a flap-and-recover loop, to keep garbage-collection pauses short because they are a leading cause of spurious evictions, to stagger maintenance so I never force mass leadership movement, and to keep the durability guards of at least two in-sync replicas and disabled unclean leader election in place so that even during unavoidable churn I never drop to an unsafe number of copies. The way I summarize it is that frequent leader movement is a symptom, and the fix is almost always to make the brokers stable and to stop moving leadership unless I intend to, while watching the leader election rate as the earliest warning sign.
